pages.text: On Monday morning in Koforidua, rain drummed loudly on the metal roof of the Primary Five classroom. ‘That was the biggest rainstorm of the whole year!’ declared Kojo at break time. Ten-year-old Akosua looked at the puddles in the yard. ‘It sounded loud on the roof, Kojo, but how do we know how much rain actually fell?’
sentences: On Monday morning in Koforidua, rain drummed loudly on the metal roof of the Primary Five classroom.
‘That was the biggest rainstorm of the whole year!’ declared Kojo at break time.
Ten-year-old Akosua looked at the puddles in the yard.
‘It sounded loud on the roof, Kojo, but how do we know how much rain actually fell?’
pages.alt: Akosua and Kojo stand on the school veranda in Koforidua watching rain drip from the roof into puddles.

pages.text: Kojo pointed to a wide flat basin under the roof gutter and a narrow bucket under the mango tree. ‘Let us just look in those!’ he said. Their science teacher, Mr Boateng, walked over shaking his head with a smile. ‘If a basin sits under a roof gutter or a dripping tree, it catches extra runoff. And if containers have different openings and slanted sides, we cannot compare the depth fairly!’
sentences: Kojo pointed to a wide flat basin under the roof gutter and a narrow bucket under the mango tree.
‘Let us just look in those!’ he said.
Their science teacher, Mr Boateng, walked over shaking his head with a smile.
‘If a basin sits under a roof gutter or a dripping tree, it catches extra runoff.
And if containers have different openings and slanted sides, we cannot compare the depth fairly!’
pages.alt: Mr Boateng points out why a basin under a dripping roof gutter and a bucket under a tree give unfair rainfall readings.

pages.text: Mr Boateng showed the class a standard rain gauge from the school weather station. It had a funnel leading into a straight-sided clear measuring cylinder marked in millimetres. ‘Meteorologists at the Ghana Meteorological Agency measure rainfall depth in millimetres,’ he explained. ‘One millimetre of rain means that if the water did not soak in or flow away, it would form a layer one millimetre deep on flat ground.’
sentences: Mr Boateng showed the class a standard rain gauge from the school weather station.
It had a funnel leading into a straight-sided clear measuring cylinder marked in millimetres.
‘Meteorologists at the Ghana Meteorological Agency measure rainfall depth in millimetres,’ he explained.
‘One millimetre of rain means that if the water did not soak in or flow away, it would form a layer one millimetre deep on flat ground.’
pages.alt: Mr Boateng holds up a clear cylindrical rain gauge with a funnel while Akosua examines the scale with her ruler.

pages.text: Together, Akosua and Kojo set up the rain gauge on a sturdy post in the middle of the open school grass, far away from buildings and trees so wind and splash would not spoil the reading. ‘Every morning at eight o’clock,’ said Akosua, opening her weather logbook, ‘we will kneel to eye level, read the bottom curve of the water, write it down, and empty the cylinder for the next day.’
sentences: Together, Akosua and Kojo set up the rain gauge on a sturdy post in the middle of the open school grass, far away from buildings and trees so wind and splash would not spoil the reading.
‘Every morning at eight o’clock,’ said Akosua, opening her weather logbook, ‘we will kneel to eye level, read the bottom curve of the water, write it down, and empty the cylinder for the next day.’
pages.alt: Akosua and Kojo mount the rain gauge on a wooden post in an open grassy area of the school compound.

pages.text: Their five-day rainfall investigation began! Monday morning’s storm had left twelve millimetres of water in the cylinder. On Tuesday, the sun shone all day, so the reading was zero millimetres. On Wednesday, steady afternoon rain fell without loud thunder, filling the gauge to eighteen millimetres!
sentences: Their five-day rainfall investigation began!
Monday morning’s storm had left twelve millimetres of water in the cylinder.
On Tuesday, the sun shone all day, so the reading was zero millimetres.
On Wednesday, steady afternoon rain fell without loud thunder, filling the gauge to eighteen millimetres!
pages.alt: Akosua kneels at eye level to read the water depth in the rain gauge cylinder while Kojo holds the weather logbook.

pages.text: Kojo looked surprised on Wednesday. ‘Monday’s storm had much louder thunder, yet Wednesday brought eighteen millimetres while Monday only brought twelve! Subtracting twelve from eighteen shows Wednesday had six millimetres more rain!’ ‘That is why scientists measure instead of guessing from noise,’ smiled Akosua.
sentences: Kojo looked surprised on Wednesday.
‘Monday’s storm had much louder thunder, yet Wednesday brought eighteen millimetres while Monday only brought twelve!
Subtracting twelve from eighteen shows Wednesday had six millimetres more rain!’ ‘That is why scientists measure instead of guessing from noise,’ smiled Akosua.
pages.alt: Kojo looks surprised at the higher water level in the cylinder while Akosua smiles and points to her notebook.

pages.text: On Thursday, a light morning shower measured six millimetres. On Friday, an evening downpour measured fourteen millimetres. In class, Akosua drew a neat bar graph on the board with the five days along the bottom and millimetres up the side. Then the class added all five days together: twelve plus zero, plus eighteen, plus six, plus fourteen equalled fifty millimetres in total!
sentences: On Thursday, a light morning shower measured six millimetres.
On Friday, an evening downpour measured fourteen millimetres.
In class, Akosua drew a neat bar graph on the board with the five days along the bottom and millimetres up the side.
Then the class added all five days together: twelve plus zero, plus eighteen, plus six, plus fourteen equalled fifty millimetres in total!
pages.alt: Akosua draws a colourful five-bar rainfall graph on the classroom board while Mr Boateng and Kojo check the total.

pages.text: ‘If we received fifty millimetres of rain across five days,’ asked Mr Boateng, ‘what was the average, or mean, rainfall per day?’ Kojo divided fifty by five in his head. ‘Ten millimetres per day!’ he answered. ‘Look how clearly the bar graph shows the wettest day, the driest day, and the pattern across the week.’
sentences: ‘If we received fifty millimetres of rain across five days,’ asked Mr Boateng, ‘what was the average, or mean, rainfall per day?’ Kojo divided fifty by five in his head.
‘Ten millimetres per day!’ he answered.
‘Look how clearly the bar graph shows the wettest day, the driest day, and the pattern across the week.’
pages.alt: Kojo raises his hand happily to answer while Akosua points to the bar graph.

pages.text: ‘Does one rainy week in June mean Koforidua’s climate has changed?’ asked Akosua. ‘No,’ said Mr Boateng. ‘Weather is what the atmosphere does from day to day, like Monday’s storm or Tuesday’s sunshine. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather measured over thirty years or more! For example, southern Ghana has two rainy seasons each year, while northern Ghana has one long rainy season, followed by the dry Harmattan wind.’
sentences: ‘Does one rainy week in June mean Koforidua’s climate has changed?’ asked Akosua.
‘No,’ said Mr Boateng.
‘Weather is what the atmosphere does from day to day, like Monday’s storm or Tuesday’s sunshine.
Climate is the long-term pattern of weather measured over thirty years or more!
For example, southern Ghana has two rainy seasons each year, while northern Ghana has one long rainy season, followed by the dry Harmattan wind.’
pages.alt: Mr Boateng points to a map of Ghana showing the rainy forest zone in the south and the savannah zone in the north.

pages.text: ‘When farmers and hydrologists compare thirty years of rain gauge records,’ Mr Boateng added, ‘they can see how global climate change is making some rainy seasons start later or fall in heavier bursts, and plan when to plant crops or store water.’ Akosua closed her weather logbook proudly. One small cylinder in the schoolyard had connected their class to scientists across Ghana! The end.

activities.question: Where should a rain gauge be placed to get an accurate, fair measurement of rainfall?
options: In an open space away from trees and roofs, read at eye level each morning
Directly under a roof gutter so it fills up faster
Underneath a thick mango tree out of the wind
activities.explanation: Placing the gauge in an open area prevents extra runoff from roofs or trees and avoids wind blockage.

activities.question: Monday had 12 mm of rain and Wednesday had 18 mm of rain. How many more millimetres fell on Wednesday than on Monday?
options: They had the exact same amount
activities.explanation: 18 mm − 12 mm = 6 mm more rain on Wednesday.

activities.question: Across the five days (12 mm, 0 mm, 18 mm, 6 mm, and 14 mm), what were the total rainfall and the daily average?
options: Total of 50 mm, with an average of 10 mm per day
Total of 40 mm, with an average of 8 mm per day
Total of 18 mm, with an average of 18 mm per day
Total of 100 mm, with an average of 20 mm per day
activities.explanation: 12 + 0 + 18 + 6 + 14 = 50 mm total; 50 mm ÷ 5 days = 10 mm per day.

activities.definition: The long-term pattern of weather in a place, measured over thirty years or more.
distractors: A single afternoon thunderstorm on a Monday
The plastic funnel on top of a rain gauge

activities.prompt: How do thirty-year rainfall records help Ghanaian farmers and dam engineers make good decisions?
Put Akosua’s scientific investigation steps in order.
items: Akosua asks how to measure which day truly had the heaviest rain.
The class sets up a rain gauge in an open area away from trees.
Akosua and Kojo record the rainfall in millimetres at 8:00 a.m. daily.
They draw a five-day bar graph and find the total and average.

activities.prompt: How did Kojo show a good scientific attitude when the measurements proved his first guess wrong?

glossary.definition: Rainwater that flows over roofs or the ground instead of soaking in.
Units of length (one-thousandth of a metre) used to measure rainfall depth.
A central value found by adding quantities together and dividing by how many there are.
The state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time from day to day.
The average pattern of weather in a region over a long period, typically thirty years or more.
